samples.summary: Hand-rolled redirect following relies on `redirect: 'manual'` exposing status + `location`; under a spec-conformant opaque-redirect filter this yields status 0 / empty headers and every redirected image fetch fails
samples.evidence: `const res = await fetchOrThrow(target, { redirect: 'manual' }, fetchImpl); const location = res.headers.get('location'); if (REDIRECT_STATUSES.has(res.status) && location) {...}`. The WHATWG spec says a `manual` redirect produces an *opaque-redirect filtered response*: type `opaqueredirect`, status `0`, empty header list, null body. If Node's undici applies that filter (it is at minimum version-dependent), `res.status` is 0 and `location` is null, so the branch is never taken and control falls to `if (!res.ok) throw httpError(res.status, 'Image fetch failed: 0  for …')`. Any image `src` served behind a CDN/http→https 301 (a normal case: the previous code used the default `redirect: 'follow'` and worked) would then fail the whole export. Every test in `packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts` stubs `fetch` with a hand-built `Response`, so the suite cannot detect this — the real transport is never exercised. Worth confirming against the pinned undici/Node version before merge.

samples.summary: `sawUnboundCallback` is set by *any* stray request to the loopback callback, so an ordinary login timeout is misreported as "the server predates nonce-bound CLI login" and misclassified as a system error (exit 2)
samples.evidence: In the request handler, `if (!nonce || !nonceMatches(nonce, expectedNonce)) { sawUnboundCallback = true; … }` fires for any request carrying a `code` but not the right nonce — including a local port scanner, another tool, or a hostile page probing the port (exactly the attacker the nonce defends against). The timeout at line 362 then branches on that flag and reports `EXIT_SYSTEM_ERROR` with the message "the server predates nonce-bound CLI login. Upgrade the server", even when the real cause was the user simply not completing the OAuth flow (which should be `EXIT_USER_ERROR`, per the branch's own else). The flag conflates "a nonce-less callback from *our* server" with "any unbound request", which the code has no way to distinguish.

samples.summary: A new CLI against a server that does not echo the nonce hangs for the full 30 s timeout instead of failing fast, and the browser is left on a bare `403 Invalid login nonce`
samples.evidence: The nonce check refuses the callback without settling (`return;` at line 314), so the only way out is the 30 s `setTimeout` at line 362. During the entire upgrade window (published CLI updates before a server deploy, or a user pointing `--server` at an older self-hosted instance) every `wafflebase login` blocks for 30 seconds, having already minted and abandoned a server-side OAuth code. The failure mode is knowable the instant a code-bearing, nonce-less callback arrives from the OAuth redirect; nothing settles the promise then.

samples.summary: The new SSRF gate blocks legitimate image hosts on private networks, breaking doc/slides export for on-prem deployments whose image origin differs from the configured `--server`
samples.evidence: `if (addresses.some(isPrivateAddress)) throw blocked(...)`. The only internal exemption is the configured server itself, and only when `effectivePort(url) === effectivePort(server)` *and* the addresses intersect (`mayBeServer`/`sharesAddressWithServer`, lines 299-312). An intranet deployment that stores absolute image URLs on a second internal host (e.g. `https://cdn.corp/...` resolving to 10.x, or a dev MinIO on `http://localhost:9000` while `--server` is `:3000` — explicitly asserted as blocked by the new test at test/image-fetcher.test.ts 'does not extend the server exemption to another port on that host') will now fail export with `IMAGE_URL_BLOCKED` where it previously succeeded. The common backend-proxied path (`/api/v1/.../images/<id>` resolved against `serverBase`) is unaffected, so this is a regression only for split-origin setups.

samples.summary: `classifiedFontFetch` discards a `Request` input's method/headers/body, forwarding only its URL plus the (absent) `init`
samples.evidence: `return async (input, init) => { const url = typeof input === 'string' ? input : input instanceof URL ? input.href : input.url; const res = await fetchOrThrow(url, init, impl); … }`. When `input` is a `Request`, all of its method, headers, body and credentials are dropped because only `input.url` survives and `init` is `undefined` in that calling convention. The wrapper is typed as `typeof globalThis.fetch`, so it is contractually usable that way; today only `PdfFonts.defaultSource` calls it (`this.fetchImpl(url)` with a string), so this is latent rather than firing — but any future caller passing a `Request` silently loses the request.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described: image-fetcher.ts:363-367 fetches with `{ redirect: 'manual' }`, :369-370 gates redirect following on `REDIRECT_STATUSES.has(res.status) && location`, and :383-388 throws `httpError(res.status, ...)` otherwise. The production path uses the platform fetch (`opts.fetch ?? globalThis.fetch`, :348) with no override at either real call site (commands/docs.ts:273, commands/slides.ts:214) and no custom undici dispatcher anywhere in packages/**, so the runtime transport is Node's bundled undici (.nvmrc 22, engines >=20). There is no handling of an `opaqueredirect`/status-0 response anywhere in the file, so IF undici applies the WHATWG opaque-redirect filter, the redirect branch is dead and every redirected image fails the export. I could not resolve that runtime question from the repository: node_modules is not vendored, so undici's `httpFetch` redirect switch is unreadable here. My library recollection is that undici deliberately returns the actual 3xx response (which would make the finding moot), but that is not grounded in any file in this working tree, and the finding's premise is precisely version-dependent. The test suite cannot discriminate either, since every case (e.g. test/image-fetcher.test.ts:360-411) hand-builds a `Response` with a literal 302 + location header. No named refutation ground applies: the code is present, unguarded, and on a real path, so the finding stays.
